content: The Burnet Institute in Melbourne, Australia, is represented by Leanne Jones, a Research Associate affiliated with the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Editorial Office at the University of Liverpool, United Kingdom. Frances Kellie serves as the Managing Editor of the same group, while Myfanwy Williams is also a Research Associate within this editorial office. The External Review Group (ERG) includes Ayse Akin from the Department of Public Health, Faculty of Medicine, Baskent University, Ankara, Turkey, and Justus Hofmeyr from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of Botswana, Gaborone, Botswana, as well as the University of the Witwatersrand and Fort Hare in East London, South Africa. Tina Lavender, from the Centre for Global Women’s Health at the University of Manchester, School of Nursing, Midwifery, and Social Work, Manchester, United Kingdom, is also a member. Suneeta Mittal represents the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Haryana, India. Alan Tita, from the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Division and Center for Women’s Reproductive Health, Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, University of Alabama at Birmingham, USA, is another contributor. Khalid Yunis, a Professor of Pediatrics and Head of the Division of Neonatology at the American University of Beirut, Lebanon, is also involved. John Varallo, the Global Director of Safe Surgery at Jhpiego, an affiliate of Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, Maryland, USA, is part of the team. WHO Country and Regional Officers include Bremen De Mucio, focusing on Sexual and Reproductive Health at the WHO Regional Office of the Americas in Montevideo, Uruguay; Karima G. Holbzour, working on Sexual and Reproductive Health at the WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean in Cairo, Egypt; Chandani Anoma Jayathilaka, specializing in Family Health, Gender, and Life Course at the WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia in New Delhi, India; Oleg K. Uzmenko, from the Division of Country Health Programmes at the WHO Regional Office for Europe in Copenhagen, Denmark; Leopold O. Uedraogo, focusing on Reproductive, Maternal Health, and Ageing at the WHO Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville, Democratic Republic of the Congo; and Howard Sobel, working on Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific in Manila, Philippines. Claudio Sosa, from the WHO Regional Office of the Americas in Montevideo, Uruguay, is also a contributor. The WHO Steering Group includes Mercedes Bonet, a Medical Officer specializing in Maternal and Perinatal Health, Sexual and Reproductive Health; Doris Chou, another Medical Officer in the same field; Tina Lavin, a Technical Officer in Maternal and Perinatal Health; Olufemi T. Oladapo, the Unit Head for Maternal and Perinatal Health; and Joshua P. Vogel, a Consultant in Maternal and Perinatal Health. Maurice Bucagu, a Medical Officer in the Maternal Health Unit, and Christine Francis, a Consultant in the Department of Surveillance, Prevention, and Control, are also part of the team. The WHO recommendations on the choice of antiseptic agents and methods of application for preoperative skin preparation for cesarean sections were developed with input from external experts and WHO staff. The recommendations prioritize outcomes such as severe infectious morbidity (e.g., sepsis, septic shock, laparotomy/hysterectomy for infection, maternal ICU admission), puerperal infection (e.g., endometritis with or without myometritis or salpingitis causing maternal febrile morbidity), and surgical site infections. Other important outcomes include maternal death, cost of care, allergy or irritation at the operation site, maternal satisfaction, maternal well-being, neonatal infection, and severe neonatal morbidity. The evidence for these recommendations was derived from a Cochrane systematic review of 13 trials involving 6,938 women. The trials compared different antiseptic agents and methods of application for preoperative skin preparation. Eight trials compared chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX) with alcohol versus povidone-iodine (PVP-I) in aqueous or alcohol-based solutions. One trial compared parachlorometaxylenol with PVP-I versus PVP-I alone, and another trial compared isopropyl alcohol scrub plus iodophor-impregnated incise drape versus iodophor scrub alone. The trials varied in their settings, populations, and definitions of outcomes, with most conducted in the USA, Egypt, India, Indonesia, and Nigeria. The review found that CHX with alcohol may reduce surgical site infections compared to PVP-I, but the evidence was of low certainty. It is unclear whether CHX reduces skin irritation or allergic reactions compared to PVP-I. Similarly, the effects of parachlorometaxylenol with PVP-I and isopropyl alcohol scrub with iodophor-impregnated drape on surgical site infections and puerperal infections remain uncertain due to very low certainty evidence. Maternal satisfaction, maternal well-being, and cost of care were not reported in the included studies. Subgroup analyses by type of antiseptic solution (alcohol-based versus aqueous-based) did not identify significant differences, but the small number of studies and imbalanced subgroup sizes limit the reliability of these findings. Further research is needed to clarify the effects of different antiseptic agents and methods of application on maternal and neonatal outcomes.
